title: Threads argument not considered with kdotpy.run()
description:
The number of threads for SciPy, umfpack, and pyMKL must be set at import. A custom number of threads can be set with a command-line argument: In `diagonalization/diagsolver.py`, we set
```py
import_num_threads = cmdargs.threads()
...
environ['OMP_NUM_THREADS'] = '%d' % import_num_threads if import_num_threads is not None else '1'
environ['MKL_NUM_THREADS'] = '%d' % import_num_threads if import_num_threads is not None else '1'
```
before we import the packages containing the diagonalization solvers (like SciPy).

This mechanism can only work if the command line is given before the modules are imported. A script like
```py
import kdotpy
kdotpy.run(*args)
```
doesn't know the number of threads at import time. If the `threads` argument is in `args`, it will be parsed only after the imports, i.e., too late.

I've come across the package `threadpoolctl` which might solve this problem. It allows to set the number of threads for example for BLAS at runtime. See https://github.com/joblib/threadpoolctl for more information.

title: Improve the interpolation between layers at the interfaces
description:
Currently, every material parameter is interpolated at an interface using a tangent hyperbola.

A more physically accurate model for the Gamma parameter would be to interpolate the valence band masses and warping instead of the Gamma parameter directly.

Other material parameters that need to be corrected when used in the Kane model, such as ge and kappa, would also benefit from an interpolation in their non-corrected form.

title: Feature request: Bandstructure of Superlattices
description:
Add the capability to kdotpy to calculate the bandstructure of superlattices. Currently, obtaining the bandstructure of superlattices involves simulating numerous single layers, which is obviously resource-intensive (especially time-consuming).

Superlattices are a special case of 2D materials, so these proposed feature should belong to kdotpy-2d and kdotpy-ll.


Upon initial investigation of the code base, I found that the following needs to be done:

- [ ] Modify the LayerStack class in layerstack.py to allow for cyclic repeating material parameters. Currently it assumes that there is vacuum at the bounders.
- [ ] According to [Vurgaftman](https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780198767275.001.0001) the FDM-Hamiltonien for superlattices needs to also include the matrix elements 1,N and N,1. Maybe this can be done with a modified version of h_constructor in hamiltonian.py.

This list is most likely not complete. Please feel free to edit this issue description and add items to the list if you find that other things need to be done.

title: Use starting vectors for sparse eigensolvers
description:
Some eigen solvers, such as SciPy and CuPy, support the setting of starting vectors. If none are set, a random unit vector is usually used instead. JAX does not currently support setting starting values. 

To speed up the calculation of the eigenvalues for B ≠ 0 and k ≠ 0, we could use the eigenvalues for B = 0 and k = 0 as the initial values, since these are calculated in advance.

title: Add a renormalisation function for material parameters.
description:
Some time ago, I encountered a problem with the simulation (not in CdHgTe) that resulted in oscillatory spurious solutions. These were clearly visible in the k-dispersion.

@mhofer eliminated the problem by performing a parameter renormalisation as proposed by [Bradley A. Foreman](https://journals.aps.org/prb/pdf/10.1103/PhysRevB.56.R12748). 

However, the Foreman paper does not use the exact same Hamiltonian as we do. The proposed approach can be summarised as follows:

- Setting the conduction band mass parameter `F=0`.
- Adjusting the Kane matrix element `P` to get the same effective mass of the conduction band as before.
- Adjusting the corrected Luttinger parameters, such that the $\Gamma8$ masses also stay constant.

As this was very useful to me, I propose that we implement such a feature in our Kdotpy software.

title: Organize functionality for vectors and for observables into subdirectories
description:
The source files `momentum.py` and `observables.py` have become increasingly large and probably get more maintainable when they're split up into multiple files. Given than the root source directory (`src/kdotpy`) already contains a lot of files, it would be preferred to organize them into subdirectories. With the appropriate `__init__.py` files, imports can stay largely the same.

- The submodule `momentum` should be renamed `vector`, which would be a more appropriate name. That is, the subdirectory name should become `vector`,  not `momentum`. The contents would then probably become:
  ```
  vector/__init__.py
  vector/vector.py            # Vector class and related functions
  vector/vectorgrid.py        # VectorGrid class and related functions
  vector/transformations.py   # VectorTransformation class, ZippedKB class, and related functions
  vector/tools.py             # optionally, for helper functions
  ```

- The submodule `observable` would be split up into the subdirectory with this name. Its contents would become:
  ```
  observables/__init__.py
  observables/base.py         # Observable class, ObservableList class
  observables/functions.py    # observable functions
  observables/observables.py  # observable definitions, all_observables global definition, observables() function
  observables/tools.py        # optionally, for helper functions
  ```

Please let me know your opinion on this proposal. I'm open for suggestions for different structuring. Also, if this plan interferes with ongoing work you're doing now or in the near future, please speak up.

title: Unexpected behaviour of `berry` in combination with `cardens` in LL calculations
description:
I performed a LL calculation using the `berry` argument in combination with a `cardens` range specification.

# Current behaviour

The resulting $\sigma_H$ output is limited to $\pm2\times 10^{11}\,\text{cm}^{-2}$ with a $0.01\times 10^{11}\,\text{cm}^{-2}$ resolution, ignoring the range and resultion specified by `cardens`.

While it should be possible to use `dosrange` to specify the range, this is not intuitive. Furthermore, `dosrange` does not take a resolution argument, only the boundaries.

# Expected behaviour

The $\sigma_H$ calculation (at least for the csv output) should also use the `cardens` range specification.

# Possible solution

A solution could look something like this:

```diff

--- a/src/kdotpy/postprocess.py

-                       idos_val = np.arange(-densrange[1], densrange[1], 0.00001)
-               else:
-                       idos_val = np.arange(densrange[0], densrange[1], 0.00001)
+       if 'cardensrange' in opts:

title: Change awkward argument pattern of VectorGrid
description:
The argument pattern of the `VectorGrid` constructor is a bit awkward. Presently, one has to construct a `VectorGrid` instance as, for example
```py
VectorGrid('x', x_array, 'y', y_value, 'z', z_array, **kwds)
```
In some cases (for example in some member functions of `VectorGrid` that return a new instance), the argument list has to be prepared separately.

*Suggested change:*\
The following argument pattern would be more intuitive:
```py
VectorGrid(x=x_array, y=y_value, z=z_array, **kwds)
```
... and it would be possible to prepare the arguments in a dict and pass it as `VectorGrid(**vector_values, **kwds)`.

I have prepared this change in commit 17b8447 in a new branch `vectorgrid25`. The existing construction method is preserved in the class method `VectorGrid.legacy()`.

*Background:*\
The primary motivation for this change is the plan to remove the coupling between the `cmdargs` submodule and `momentum.py` in the branch `cmdargs24` (see issue #135). The function `cmdargs.vectorvalues()` should no longer return a `VectorGrid` instance, but rather a dict that allows the instance to be created elsewhere, as
```py
VectorGrid(**cmdargs.vectorvalues(...))
```

title: Incomplete preprocessed data in XML output
description:
While playing with potentials I noticed that the potential function itself is not stored in the XML output file. Upon closer inspection, I found that the potential is handled internally as a value in the `modelopts` dict. The latter is not saved into the XML file, although it contains essential data for debugging and reproducibility of results. I consider this to be problematic.

*Possible solution*:\
Write the contents of the `modelopts` dict in a suitable way to the XML file. The most sensible way to do this (keeping things compatible between versions) would be to add a new XML tag `<model_options>` directly under `<datafile>`.

If we proceed with this, it might also be worth adding `bandalign_opts` and possibly other similar containers. Here, I'm thinking specifically of "preprocessed data", i.e., values that go into the calculation. Whether additional "postprocessed data" should be added to the XML is another discussion.

description:

The corresponding `ploto` function implements the `ll_full` keyword argument to differentiate between true `1d` mode and Landau level mode.

bc2e31b6 implements a hotfix for this bug. \
There are other inconsistencies between the functions concerning the `basis`, `basislabels`, and `phase_rotate` arguments. These should be addressed while re-structuring the code such that `ploto` and `tableo` use a common data-processing method, thereby avoiding such issues in the future.

title: kdotpy help does not work in Windows
description:
The built-in help function `kdotpy help` does not work on Windows, because it relies on `less`, which is a command only available on Linux (but not on all Linux distributions).

*Possible solution:*\
Windows doesn't have `less` but it has `more`, which has significantly less functionality (ironically). The function `pydoc.pager()` chooses whichever is appropriate (i.e., generally `less` on Linux, `more` on Windows, but doesn't pass options, such as the search option `less -i --pattern=item` which is invoked if one calls `kdotpy help item`. The best solution would be to use `less` if available, and use a suitable fallback if not. For the latter, we could choose `pydoc.pager()` or dump the appropriate output to the terminal.

title: Observables based on derivatives incorrect after redoing band alignment
description:
In `kdotpy merge`, one can "realign" the data with the `bandalign` command-line argument. This is a common thing to do when merging two or more data sets into a single one.

When data sets are merged, the observable values from the source data sets are copied to the merged data set. This is completely appropriate if an observable is an expectation value. For derivatives however, the values depend on the dispersion at neighbouring k points for the same band index, so band alignment can alter the values. In other words, the copied values will (in general) no longer be valid.

*Possible solution:*\
When doing manual band alignment, the existing values of the derivatives are no longer valid and they should either be invalidated (by removing the observable or by setting the values to `NaN`) or be recalculated and replaced. Perhaps invalidation is already recommended when merging more than one data set even without doing `bandalign`: In this case, even while the band indices are not changed, adding data points would require recalculating derivatives.

I suggest to make this behaviour configurable, with at least three options:
- `recalculate`
- `invalidate`
- `keep` (as this is not recommended, a warning should be shown)

The default value could be `recalculate`, as this is not computationally expensive.

title: Compatibility with Numpy 2
description:
Currently, kdotpy is not compatible with Numpy versions 2.x.y. This is correctly listed in the dependency list in `pyproject.toml`: When one installs kdotpy 1.0.0 with `pip install`, PIP installs a version of Numpy 1.26, not 2.x.y.

As a matter of fact, the Numpy 1.x.y versions are compatible with Python versions up to 3.12. This makes kdotpy currently incompatible with the new Python 3.13, as it can never successfully install the dependencies. If one tries to do this, PIP will fetch Numpy version 1.26.y, but it will emit a build error and fail to install it.

*Proposed solution:*\
The obvious way out is to make kdotpy compatible with Numpy 2.x.y. The changes in namespace are actually not so many and are easily resolved:\
[numpy2.patch](/uploads/4e555e0883f573fba5fb60535e783b01/numpy2.patch)

The [migration to Numpy 2](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/numpy_2_0_migration_guide.html) may have some other side effects. I haven't found any so far, but I request others to also test and report unforeseen errors and/or changes in results.

title: Error when setting multiple material parameters with '_' in their names using the matparam command line option.
description:
While experimenting with porting new materials to kdotpy, I came across an error when setting multiple material parameters using the matparam command line option. This error seems to be related to material parameters with a '_' in their name. I was able to successfully reproduce this bug using the quantum well dispersion tutorial.

When I add the command line option `matparam 'HgTe:a=0.65'` to the tutorial, everything works as expected. When I now change the command line option to `matparam 'HgTe:a=0.65;delta_so=1.0e3'` I get the following error: `ERROR (MaterialsList.parse_cmdarg): Material id 'delta' does not exist.`.

A possible quick fix is to change the line to `matparam 'HgTe:a=0.65;HgTe:delta_so=1.0e3'`, this eliminates the error and changes the delta_so. 

I've also tried what happens if you use the command line option `matparam 'HgTe:a=0.65;gamma1=1.5'` and this works as expected (a and gamma1 are changed).  So I conclude that this behaviour is related to the '_' in the name of the material parameter.

title: Unintuitive handling of equations in matparam files
description:
@jkuther and I are experimenting with implementing new materials in kdotpy. Following the [materials/default](https://git.physik.uni-wuerzburg.de/kdotpy/kdotpy/-/blob/f86d64f65f2be1f57bca5cd8520860c43fffceef/src/kdotpy/materials/default) file for CdTe, we implemented a new material that includes:

```
[newmat]
Eg             = some function of T
Evoff          = -100
Ev             = Evoff
Ec             = Evoff + Eg
```

In subsequent calculations, we tried modifying the valence band offset of the material using `matparam 'newmat:Evoff=-110'`. From the definition above, we expected this would change both the material parameters `Ev` and `Ec`. However, only `Ec` is affected.

This is easily explained by looking at the `kdotpy-materials.log`, which reads:

```
[newmat]
Eg             = some function of T
Evoff          = -100
Ev             = -100
Ec             = Evoff + Eg
```

I.e. while reading in the materials file, the value of `Ev` was immediately substituted, and `Ev` is no longer a function of `Evoff`.

If one instead changes the definition in the materials file to:

```
[newmat]
Eg             = some function of T
Evoff          = -100
Ev             = Evoff + 0 * T
Ec             = Evoff + Eg
```
making `Evoff` a trivial function of temperature, `Ev` is no longer substituted upon reading in the materials file, and the `matparam` relation from above works as we have expected.

I propose that we add a note to the wiki, cautioning users that formulas that already evaluate to numerical values upon reading in the materials file are immediately resolved. I don't think it is necessary to change the current program behavior. Please discuss.

title: False negatives for thickness commensurability test
description:
Rounding errors lead to false negatives for the thickness commensurability test. For example, the combination of arguments `llayer 10.5 70 10.5 zres 0.35` leads to the error
```
ERROR (LayerStack): Thickness of the layers is not commensurate with the z resolution. Change z resolution or layer thicknesses; or set configuration option 'lattice_zres_strict=false' to ignore this error.
```
Obviously, 10.5, 70, and 10.5 are divisible by 0.35 in a formal sense. However, in floating point arithmetic, 

```
>>> 10.5/0.35
30.000000000000004
```

*Proposed solution:*\
Do not use `int(ceil(d / zres))` to determine the number of lattice points in the layers, as is currently done, but use a more sensible rounding method.

title: Using stripangle with kdotpy 1d raises TypeError
description:
If one uses `stripangle` with `kdotpy 1d`, the construction of the Hamiltonian fails with the following `TypeError`:
```
  File "/home/wbeugeling/Development/kdotpy/src/kdotpy/hamiltonian/transform.py", line 230, in is_invariant_under_transform
    new_kjt = self.transform(rr3, rr5 = rr5, in_place = False)
              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/wbeugeling/Development/kdotpy/src/kdotpy/hamiltonian/transform.py", line 196, in transform
    raise TypeError
```
The function in question receives a float where it expects an array.

The reason for this error seems to lie deeper, namely `stripangle` causes the construction of a transformable Hamiltonian. Apparently, the transformation parameters are not properly initialized in `PhysParams.__init__()`.

The following code in the Hamiltonian constructor `h1zy()` seems to be unreachable, i.e., the part below `if params.lattice_transformed_by_angle()`.
```py
	if not axial:
		# strip orientation; phase applies to non-axial term only
		if params.lattice_transformed_by_angle():
			phi = params.lattice_orientation[0] * np.pi / 180.
			kp2_phase = np.exp( 4.j * phi)
			km2_phase = np.exp(-4.j * phi)
		else:
			kp2_phase = 1.0
			km2_phase = 1.0
		rr   += -0.5 * kp2 * kp2_phase * hbarm0 * sqrt(3.) * (pp['gamma3'] - pp['gamma2']) * onez  # non-axial term
		rrd  += -0.5 * km2 * km2_phase * hbarm0 * sqrt(3.) * (pp['gamma3'] - pp['gamma2']) * onez

```

It is not clear what the intentions were at the moment this was developed. The question is, do we want to be able to use the 'simplified' code where we just add a phase? This means that for `stripangle`, one would only add this phase and bypass the construction of a transformable Hamiltonian. This may be useful for debugging and (maybe) for slightly increased performance.

In any case, the handling of the `lattice_orientation` parameter in `PhysParams.__init__()` needs to be fixed.

title: Failure when estimating CNP when high 'E' band char indices are wrong
description:
During my latest modelling runs, where I changed multiple material parameters, I noticed that estimation of the CNP regularly fails due to wrong band char indices at high energies.   
The calculations are basic LL calculations for a 30nm sample in axial approximation. (I can supply further info, if needed.)  
Determination of band index and connecting the LL states in the bdependence plots works fine. 

Here is a snippet of the determined band chars as an example:  
`[...] H1+ E2- E2- E2- E2- E2- E2- E2- E2- E2- E2- E2- E2- E2+ E2+ E2+ E2+ E2+ E2+ E2+ E2+ E2+ E2+ E2+ E3- E3- E3- E3- E3- E3- E3- E3- E3- E3- E3- E3- E3+ E3+ E3+ E3+ E3+ E3+ E3+ E3+ E3+ E3+ E3+ E4- E4- E4- E4- E4- E4- E4- E4- E4- E4- E4- E4- E4+ E4+ E4+ E4+ E4+ E4+ E4+ E4+ E4+ E4+ E4+ E5- E5- E5- E5- E5- E5- E5- E5- E5- E5- E5- E5- E5+ E5+ E5+ E5+ E5+ E5+ E5+ E5+ E5+ E5+ E5+ E6- E6- E6- E6- E6- E6- E6- E6- E6- E6- E6- E6- E6+ E6+ E6+ E6+ E6+ E6+ E6+ E6+ E6+ E6+ E6+ ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? E67- E67- E67- E67- E67- E67- E67- E67- E67- E67- E67- E67- E67+ E67+ [...]`

`estimate_charge_neutrality_point()` in `cnp.py` looks for the highest `E` band index, which is `67` in this case, and counts down band indices starting at the highest band. For the presented case this returns  
`"ERROR (estimate_charge_neutrality_point): Failed, because neutral point does not lie in energy range"`  
since `E67+-` is obviously not the 67th conduction band, judging from the band char list, and thus the estimated state index `j_above_gap = max(j_ep, j_em) + 1 - dj` is negative.

A possible solution would be to extend the functionality of one of the selector functions `check_char_in_order` or `get_confidence_window` (probably the first), to include a check on such rough index jumps and ultimately exclude them from the states used for the estimation of the CNP.

I would set this to low priority, because by using `neig` and `targetenergy` this issue can be circumvented.

title: Band alignment for full-diag self-consistent calculations
description:
While investigating full-diag self-consistent calculations for chemical potentials inside the bulk valence band, a question about the validity of the current band alignment algorithm for densz calculations came up. \
The current band alignment algorithm only produces anti-crossings, which inevitably leads to a 'wrong' band assignment when potentials push one of the surface state bands below a bulk valence band state (see the calculation presented in this comment f.e. https://git.physik.uni-wuerzburg.de/kdotpy/kdotpy/-/issues/66#note_17643).

This can lead to a wrong interpolation of the `psi2z` and/or slope of the bands for `densz` calculations.

title: Proposal: Binary output files
description:
Currently mostly csv files are used for data processing outside of kdotpy. The downside of the csv format is that it is lossy (due to the finite precision) and inefficient in terms of the file size.

Binary data files which store data in their native representation could do so more efficiently. There is no loss of precision. Due to the lack of the conversion step, it's probably also faster.

Two formats come into mind:
- The numpy data format (npz files).
- HDF5. Note that an output function is included with pandas, so implementation should be relatively straightforward.

Are these formats desired for processing data in external programs? Please discuss.\
Note that the question is specifically about data processing. Long-term data storage is a (related but) different question. For the purpose of long-term data storage, we're currently using the xml output. (Which we also wish to improve in the future.)

title: SelfConSolverLL does not handle B dependent broadening
description:
The self-consistent solver `SelfConSolverLL` can handle constant broadening, but not a broadening that depends on magnetic field B.

The problem is two-fold:
- The `SelfConSolverLL` class does not call `broadening.apply_width_dependence()` at initialization.
- For the calculation of densityz, in `densityz_ll()`, applying a B dependent broadening leads to an exception raised by `broadening.apply_idos(idos, ee)`, that the array shape of `idos` is incorrect. The latter function cannot handle the three-dimensional array `idos` (shape `(nB, nz, ne)`) correctly: It does not know what to do with the second axis over z.

*Possible solution*:\
Adapt `BroadeningFunction.apply_idos()` such that it iterates over the middle axis (axes) if the array has shape `(nB, ..., ne)`, where `...` indicates at least one intermediate axis. The application of `broadening.apply_width_dependence()` at initialization of a `SelfConSolverLL` instance is trivial to implement.

description:
The exchange coupling parameters $T_0$ and $g_\mathrm{Mn}$ (`TK0` and `gMn`) are hardcoded values in `physparams.py`.

Recently, the value of `TK0` has been challenged: New data shows that for (Hg,Mn)Te with ~2% of Mn, the value should be ~0.7 K, significantly off from the value used by [Novik et al. (2005)]. Moreover, it increases with increasing Mn concentration.

*Possible solution:*\

title: Disentangle import spaghetti
description:
The dependency graph of the internal python files is an entangled mess.

![kdotpy-dependency-graph](/uploads/bd6c136bd9c6eb31833cc84f8a6b72bf/kdotpy-dependency-graph.png)\
(for branch `packaging`)

I would like to clean this up and get a more layered structure, i.e., lasagne instead of spaghetti.

There are also a few loops in the dependency graphs, for example around `bandalign` and `diagdata`. These are better avoided.

*Possible solution:*\
Many of the dependencies are simply for type-checking, for example `DiagData` and `DiagDataPoint` from `diagdata.py`. Here, there are two ways out:
- Discard explicit type checking.
- Defining a separate Python module where an abstract base class is defined, without explicit implementations. For type checking, this module can be imported. The advantage is, that this module needs no imports of its own. Only where the class is constructed, the original module (with the implementations) is imported. Of course, the class-with-implementations needs to inherit from the base class.

This would get rid of some problematic dependencies, but not all. Further suggestions are welcome.

title: Proposal: Change strategy for matplotlibrc
description:
If nothing is specified on the command line, matplotlib loads the `matplotlibrc` if it exists in the working directory. Otherwise it defaults to the built-in default values. If the user puts a file `matplotlibrc` into the `~/.kdotpy` directory, this file will not be loaded unless the command line argument `plotrc` is given.

This behaviour is not very intuitive, and different from how materials files are going to be implemented (see branch `materialsfile`).

*Proposed changes:*
- If there's nothing specified on the command line, the default strategy for loading `matplotlibrc` parameters should become: current working directory, config directory (`~/kdotpy`), built-in values.
- Perhaps we should not provide the complete file `matplotlibrc` with the kdotpy source code. It's better to supply only a shortened version (like the [example in the Wiki](https://git.physik.uni-wuerzburg.de/wbeugeling/kdotpy/-/wikis/tutorials/customizing-graphics), or none at all.
- If we choose to provide a (shortened) `matplotlibrc` file, the best strategy seems to copy it from the source into the config directory.
- The command line argument alias `rcfile` may be confusing, as it is not clear that it refers to `matplotlibrc` and not to `kdotpyrc`. (It was defined before the configuration framework with `kdotpyrc` was implemented.) In my opinion, we should thus deprecate `rcfile`.

title: Density units not intuitive
description:
In dispersion mode, the density of states is calculated as occupied volume in momentum space and this is also the default output (plots and tables). The textbook definition of density of states is this volume divided by $(2\pi)^d$, given how reciprocal space is defined in terms of real space.
Using a non-standard definition for DOS/IDOS leads to confusion. To add even more to the confusion, the LL calculation always uses the textbook definition.

(This issue was raised by @mhofer recently, and has been mentioned in the past by others.)

*Possible solution:*\
Make the textbook definition the default one also for dispersion mode. Densities expressed as the volume in momentum space should remain available as option.

To achieve this goal:
- Change some of the implementation in the classes `DensityData` and `DensityScale`. In particular, the density values in dispersion mode need to be multiplied by the appropriate factor.
- In `DensityScale`, replace `scaletype` by two arguments: `quantity` and `unit`. The `quantity` will determine what is counted (momentum space volume, carrier density, charge density) and the `unit` will be `nm` or `cm`.
- The scaling type will no longer be a command line argument, but two configuration values `dos_quantity` and `dos_unit`. The idea is that one is unlikely to change these values between runs of kdotpy.
- Some distinctions between densities in dispersion and LL mode may be removed, as they will use the same units in the future.
- While doing this, I'll remove some inconsistencies in plot and table functions, and optimize some postprocessing functions.

title: Proposal: Define material parameters with input file
description:
There is a desire to add new materials or modify/fine-tune the parameters of materials already defined. In the current implementation, where the parameters are hardcoded in `materialsdef.py`, it would require editing this file. This approach is not very user friendly, and even more so when one does not have the permission to edit the source files.

I suggest a new implementation where the material parameters are read from separate files that can be edited and/or created by the user. 

*Possible implementation:*
- One file per material, stored in the directory `~/.kdotpy`.
- A few material files could be included with kdotpy, maybe in a separate directory in the source.
- Maybe also allow material files in the working directory.
- The syntax may be simple, one `key=value` pair per line, similar to the config file. The 'keys' are the parameters like `Ec`, `Ev`, `gamma1`, etc.
- The values should allow simple functions (such as polynomials, e.g. `0.6462 + 0.0009 * x + 0.0017 * x**2 - 0.0006 * x**3`) to model materials with a concentration parameter `x`. Also temperature dependence should be allowed. It's probably most convenient to use the `ast` module of Python to parse such function definitions.

title: Electrons vs. Holes in Our Calculations
description:
As I showed in the kdotpy-meeting on Jul 26, the self-consistent calculations currently give unphysical carrier density distribution. See f.e. this calculation with a base density (symmetric) of 0.005 e/nm^2 gated to 0.009 e/nm^2:

![densz0.009.pdf](/uploads/ac5bc9a7671804c18d866e65a789d360/densz0.009.pdf.png)

This is obviously unphysical, as one would see a large carrier mixed carrier density in experiments if this was true.

The following figure shows how the band structure evolves in the self-consistent calculations. One observes that for larger potentials, increasingly more conduction band states are pushed into the valence band states:
![comparison.pdf](/uploads/fd72f54fc22d5f33881c997f85478d2e/comparison.pdf.png)

It seems that we need to re-think what states we label as holes and what states as electrons. Currently, we are calculating the [Charge neutral point](https://git.physik.uni-wuerzburg.de/wbeugeling/kdotpy/-/wikis/physics/Charge-neutral-point) at `k=0` and label everything below the CNP as holes and everything above as electrons. These electron-like and hole-like characters of the bands are propagated to `k≠0`by the band alignment process. This means that we are f.e. labeling some of the highly dispersive states in the 0.008 e/nm^2 and 0.009 e/nm^2 calculation as hole-like even way above the chemical potential `µ`.

A discussion after our group meeting yesterday with @msiebert and @cberger lead to an alternative idea of how to differentiate bewteen hole-like and electron-like states.
The idea is based on the fact that at every `k`-point, the number of occupied states should be the same. As a lot of complicated band-crossings are happening in the gated calculations, this requires a `k`-dependent CNP. By choosing a low-lying `H` subband (below the lowest `E` subband but above the highest `L` subband) as a stable (band aligned) reference point, it is possible to simply count the (always constant) number of occupied energy eigenstates. This is equivalent to starting from very large `k`, finding the CNP there and then propagating it back to `k=0` sliding in beween states.

Carrying out the proposed `k`-dependent CNP calculation for the 0.008 e/nm^2 band strcuture from above gives the following result:
![electrons_holes.pdf](/uploads/a3539deefe70740a76420714b8fce510/electrons_holes.pdf.png)

I also already started implementing the calculation in `selfcon.py` by trying to utilize the already existing possiblity to pass an `e_neutral` array to `densityz()`. The [CNP_k.patch](/uploads/9bf405c1ed02ece87509e9456e22a3c9/CNP_k.patch) applies to 6665adc2e37c380cc005d9682f93eefc913e7576. This implementation does not work quite yet, as some functions (in particular `int_dos_by_band()` in `densitybase.py`) have an issue with bands that are not fully electron- or hole-like. I am going to work on that next.

title: Feature request: Save binary eigenvector data for kdotpy-bulk
description:
Currently the storage of eigenvector data in a binary format (numpy binary or hdf5) is not yet implemented for bulk mode.

*Suggestion*:\
Use the existing function `DiagData.to_binary_file()` for bulk mode. Note that the for the other geometries, the binary file output is done by calling `DiagDataPoint.to_binary_file()` in `models.py` for each `DiagDataPoint` separately. Due to the potentially large number of data points for bulk, it is probably wise to use the `.to_binary_file()` function in `DiagData` rather in `DiagDataPoint`.

A suitable wrapper will be needed to take care that the eigenvectors are stored in `DiagData`. It might be advisable to define a suitable `ModelBase` subclass for bulk. This also requires a test of performance, to make sure that the extra overhead is not slowing down the calculation too much. Also memory consumption should be monitored.

title: (Temperature) Broadening in Self-consistent calculations affects convergence
description:
After fixing the issue that not converged magnetic field points are replaced with the previous diagonalization results in self-consistent LL calculations in 82101a12, the overall convergence behaviour seemed unstable.   
I did some testing and found out that this is connected to the (temperature) broadening used for the calculation. The convergence behaviour strongly depends on the temperature value or if broadening is used at all.   
The command line in question is:
```
kdotpy-ll.py 8o erange -100 100 b 0 5 // 10 zres 0.25 targetenergy 10 nll 10 neig 150 split 0.01 llayer 10 12 10 mlayer HgCdTe 68% HgTe HgCdTe 68% msubst CdTe ax char legend cardens 0.001 dos selfcon 100 0.01 selfconweight 0.9 config lattice_regularization=false;selfcon_debug=true;selfcon_dynamic_time_step=true;selfcon_convergent_steps=2;selfcon_erange_from_eivals=true;transitions_spectra=false transitions obs llindex
```

- **no broadening**: converged after 5 iterations
- **dostemp 1.5**: did not fully converge after 50 iterations (8/11 points converged)
- **dostemp 5**: converged after 18 iterations
- **dostemp 10**: did not fully converge after 50 iterations (10/11 points converged)

Which magnetic field points converge seems random.   
We would expect that convergence behaviour would improve with activated broadening, since determination of the electro-chemical potential should be more accurate for broadened LLs (no delta function) for fixed energy resolution. This is apparently not the case.   

I implemented a temporary workaround in 91fbb079, where broadening can be en-/disabled by setting `config selfcon_ll_use_broadening=true/false` for the self-consistent calculation only.

Nevertheless, we should investigate why broadening worsens convergence behaviour and if this is connected to how (temperature) broadening is implemented at the moment.

title: CI/CD job artifacts don't expire
description:
The so-called artifacts (files generated by CI/CD jobs) pile up. They constitute more than half of the storage space of this Gitlab project.

The expiry time for job artifacts is not set in `.gitlab-ci.yml`, which would normally mean that it uses the expiry time set by the Gitlab instance. Seemingly, this instance does not set an expiry time.

*Suggested solution*:\
Set an expiry time in `.gitlab-ci.yml`. The "default" time of 30 days should be workable. The existing job artifacts (generated till now) shall be deleted.

title: Confusing labelling of Fermi energy
description:
Currently, the "special energies" dict contains `ef` (rendered in plots as $`E_\mathrm{F}`$), meaning the Fermi level at zero density, and `mu` (rendered as $`\mu`$), meaning the Fermi level or chemical potential at the given density. This is not the meaning one finds in textbooks, and the labels tend to confuse.

For finite temperatures, $`\mu`$ would be the conventional notation for the Fermi level at any temperature. However:

> [...] in semiconductor textbooks it is often denoted by the symbol $`\epsilon_\mathrm{F}`$.

[Hook and Hall, *Solid state physics*, second edition]

> In semiconductor theory the electron chemical potential is always called the **Fermi level**. Further, in semiconductor theory the character $`\mu`$ is almost always reserved for the electron and hole mobilities, and the Fermi level is designated by $`\epsilon_\mathrm{F}`$ or by $`\zeta`$.

[Kittel and Kroemer, *Thermal Physics*, second edition]

Alright...

*Possible solution:*\
In any case, we should use a consistent notation for both Fermi level at given and zero density, where the latter should get an extra 0 (subscript). Would anyone have a clear preference for either of the following two choices?
1. `ef` and `ef0` ($`E_\mathrm{F}`$ and $`E_{\mathrm{F},0}`$; or $`\epsilon_\mathrm{F}`$ and $`\epsilon_{\mathrm{F},0}`$)
2. `mu` and `mu0` ($`\mu`$ and $`\mu_0`$)

Also other suggestions are welcome.

(for comparison: [`ArpackNoConvergence` Doc](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.sparse.linalg.ArpackNoConvergence.html#scipy.sparse.linalg.ArpackNoConvergence) and [multiprocessing breaks when payload fails to unpickle](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/83932))


This behaviour can be reproduced by using the commandline (tested on commit 34062e0d)    
`8o msubst CdZnTe 4% mlayer HgCdTe 68% HgTe HgCdTe 68% llayer 10 7 10 zres 0.1 b 0 2 // 10 nll 10 neig 200 split 0.01 ax targetenergy 10 config "luttinger_gamma1=0;luttinger_gamma2=0;luttinger_gamma3=0;luttinger_kappa=0;luttinger_F=0;luttinger_q=0" cpu 7`   
and applying [Luttinger_as_cmd_parameters.patch](/uploads/2824dd35798d40eb1c702961f300e970/Luttinger_as_cmd_parameters.patch).

I could only reproduce this with the combinations of `zres 0.1 targetenergy 10 cpu 7` and the given config values for Luttinger parameters using the patch. Changing a single value or don't setting Luttinger parameter via patch won't result in an infinite loop.   
Based on the fact, that this behaviour is highly situational, I think this issue is not of high priority.

title: DOS validity range rules too strict
description:
The DOS validity range is obtained by verifying which bands go up and which go down at the boundaries of the calculated momentum range. The validity range then spans the energy of the highest band going down (valence band behaviour) until the energy of the lowest band going up (conduction band behaviour).

For complicated band structures, e.g., 3D TIs, the subbands dispersions may wiggle up and down as a result of mutual hybridization (see figure). This leads to a "band going up" for an energy deep in the valence band, so the validity range limit is set to that energy. In this case, the "upper" limit of the validity range is -192 meV, which happens to be the lowest band in the calculation (and it goes up at k = 0.4 nm<sup>-1</sup>). The expected result is 142 meV, where the lowest conduction band dispersion at  k = 0.4 nm<sup>-1</sup>. Note that the "lower limit" of the validity range is set correctly at -14 meV.

*Possible solution*:\
Work out an algorithm that uses extrapolation of the dispersions to a specific (large) k value. Possibly, one needs to take into account band indices as well.

![dispersion-3dti-vb-up](/uploads/e8060674675956ff82eb2f7d7d7edda6/dispersion-3dti-vb-up.png)\
Figure was produced using:
```
kdotpy 2d 8o noax strain 0.3% mater HgCdTe 68% HgTe HgCdTe 68% llayer 10 70 10 zres 0.2 split 0.0001 k 0 0.4 / 80 kphi 0 targetenergy 10 neig 80 char legend dos erange -120 20
```

title: Axis argument to 'strain' does not do what users expect
description:
The second argument argument to `strain` was originally meant for allowing to rotate the "strain axis" into the x direction. The effect of `strain <epsilon> x` sets the diagonal components of the strain tensor $`(\epsilon_{xx},\epsilon_{yy},\epsilon_{zz})=(\epsilon',\epsilon,\epsilon)`$, where $`\epsilon`$ is the specified in-plane strain and $`\epsilon'=-2\frac{C_{12}}{C_{11}}\epsilon`$. For the default strain axis the result would be $`(\epsilon,\epsilon,\epsilon')`$.

The argument sequence `strain <epsilon> x` is easily misinterpreted as "set $`\epsilon_{xx}=\epsilon`$", rather opposite of what it should be used for.

*Possible solution*:\
Remove the argument `strain_dir`. Instead, allow `strain` to take multiple numerical values, interpreted as $`\epsilon_{xx},\epsilon_{zz}`$ (2 values) or $`\epsilon_{xx},\epsilon_{yy},\epsilon_{zz}`$ (3 arguments).

title: Unrecognized configuration keys in kdotpyrc are lost
description:
If kdotpy is run and there are unrecognized configuration keys, those are lost when kdotpy rewrites the configuration file.

I discovered this issue while changing between the branches `densityz` and `develop`. The branch `density` has many new configuration keys related to the new implementation of the self-consistent calculation, that are not yet in `develop`. After switching from `densityz` to `develop` and running `kdotpy`, the new configuration keys disappear from `kdotpyrc`.

The problem applies to `newkey=value` as well as `# newkey=value`, i.e., without and with comment sign `#`.

*Possible solution:*\
Instead of writing the complete file every time `kdotpy` is run, only append new configuration keys to the existing instance of `kdotpyrc`.

title: Redesign self-consistent calculation
description:
@cberger and @wbeugeling are presently working on re-designing the code for self-consistent calculation. This issue is to keep track of this work. Also see issue #4 for earlier discussion and merge request !6 for the previous efforts (by @fbayer foremost). I have opened a new issue, because this a new attempt and we would like to document especially this. Work is now done in branch `densityz`.

*Motivation:*\
The new implementation of `densityz()` (see issue #75) has already brought a great improvement to the stability of the self-consistent Hartree calculation. The suspicion that the discrepancy between the old version of `densityz()` and `integrated_dos()` has led to convergence problems with the self-consistent calculation, has proved to be true.

*Suggested implementation:*\
We're using the improvement of `densityz()` as an opportunity to (finally) make a complete effort towards a stable implementation of the self-consistent calculation. We're taking inspiration from the earlier efforts in `adiabatic-selfcon` (merge request !6) and the discussion in issue #4.

The first focus is the 'dispersion' variant `hartree_potential()`. The LL version `hartree_potential_ll()` shall be dealt with later.

*List of tasks:*
- [x]  Estimate of CNP is not reliable in a strong potential. Fix it by estimating it for zero potential, then increase the potential adiabatically. (Work in branch `adiabatic-bandinit`.)
- [x]  Verify the convergence behaviour of the existing implementation (with the new `densityz()`).
- [ ]  Apply task manager / workload distribution system (by @fbayer) to diagonalizations.
- [x]  Define class for self-consistent calculation. It should store all relevant input and output, as well as provide functions for doing the iteration and checking convergence. See also https://git.physik.uni-wuerzburg.de/wbeugeling/kdotpy/-/merge_requests/6#note_14001.
- [x]  Implement more advanced convergence checks.
- [ ]  Implement more advanced iterators, that take into account "more history" than just the last step: That is, `vz` at iteration `n` is calculated not only from `vz` at iteration `n - 1`, but possibly also from iterations `n - k` with k > 1.
- [x]  Add the option to input initial potential or density distribution.
- [x]  Redesign the LL version with the new class infrastructure. Ideally, the new class should be common to both versions. We'd like to reduce the amount of code duplication.
- [x]  Optimize the LL version. In particular, use the idea of reducing work load by skipping data points where convergence has been reached already. (See !6 and https://git.physik.uni-wuerzburg.de/wbeugeling/kdotpy/-/issues/4#note_7806)
- [ ]  Evaluate if the idea of `adiabatic-selfcon` using band alignment between iterations should be implemented.

(further tasks may be added)

title: Densityz vs integrated DOS
description:
The functions `densityz()` and `integrated_dos()` work in different ways. This affects the self-consistent Hartree calculation foremost.

*Details:*\
The function `densityz()` uses the occupation functions at the energy eigenvalues at the data points only:
```py
occ = brf.occupation(eival - e_f, index = j)
```
In contrast, `integrated_dos()` calculates the density considering linear interpolation between the data points; see the functions `*_idos_element()` in `densityelements.py`. As a result, the results of `np.sum(densityz()) * dz` and `integrated_dos()` are not exactly the same.

This discrepancy particularly affects the self-consistent Hartree calculation in the following way. The self-consistent algorithm extracts the Fermi energy from the result of `integrated_dos()` for the given density `cardens`. Then, it calculates `densityz()` at this Fermi energy. The discrepancy manifests itself as a deviation of `np.sum(densityz()) * dz` from the expected value `cardens`. Presently, the self-consistent algorithm compensates by applying a multiplicative factor, but this cannot be done in the limit of zero `cardens`.

*Possible solution:*\
The function `densityz()` should also take the occupations from the `*_idos_element()` functions of `densityelements.py`. Just like `integrated_dos()`, an integral should be performed using the integration elements in `densityelements.py`, but with an extra factor that encodes $`|\psi_i(z)|^2`$ for each eigenstate. For the latter, several options are possible:
-  For each element, use the average of the $`|\psi_i(z_j)|^2`$ at the corners (or ends) $`z_j`$. (*relatively easy*)
-  Incorporate $`|\psi_i(z_j)|^2`$ at the corners (or ends) directly in the calculation of the occupation function. (*more difficult, both conceptually and computationally*)

*Solution strategy:*\
We should try implementing the *relatively easy* solution first. After it's done, it needs to be checked that `np.sum(densityz()) * dz` yields the same result as `integrated_dos()`, at least up to numerical accuracy. If that is the case, we can use it in the self-consistent calculation and see if it increases stability. Note that if this is successful, the self-consistent algorithm can be simplified substantially,  as `integrated_dos()` and the correction factors then become superfluous.

title: Proposal: Configuration tool
description:
It might be useful to have a configuration tool `kdotpy config` to easily view, set, and get information about configuration options.

*Possible implementation:*\
The tool should be a python script `kdotpy-config.py` that can also be invoked using the `kdotpy` master script as `kdotpy config`. The syntax should be roughly similar to `git config`. It should be able to do the following:
- `kdotpy config <key>` to view the value for `<key>`.
- `kdotpy config <key>=<value>` to set the value for `<key>`.
- `kdotpy config reset <key>` to set `<key>` back to its default value.
- `kdotpy config help <key>` to view the information about `<key>` from `README`.
- `kdotpy config file` to output the filename of the configuration file.
- `kdotpy config edit` to open the configuration file in an editor.

I would also like to see an option to apply these actions to a local configuration file, using a modifier `local`, e.g., `kdotpy config local <key>=<value>`. Whether we should require an explicit modifier for the global configuration is point of discussion. Concatenating multiple keys like `<key>=<value>;<key>=<value>` should be possible.

title: Proposal: Compatibility with older Python and module versions
description:
Currently, we have not specified version compatibility very clearly. The Wiki states:
> As far as I can see, `kdotpy` is presently compatible with Python version ≥ 3.5.0. Earlier versions of Python 3 do not need to be supported. Compatibility with versions 3.5.x, 3.6.x, and newer should be maintained. Thus, constructs that are not valid in 3.5.x (etc.), but only in newer versions, should be avoided.

Meanwhile, the oldest version of Python still receiving support is 3.7.x. Also, the statement does not say anything about module/library versions. Lack of clarity about compatibility requirements can sometimes be an obstacle towards using optimized features of newer versions: In my own experience, when using a feature that is listed as "New since library version x.y", I feel unsure about being able to use it. Having clear version compatibility statements avoids this issue.

*Suggestion*:\
I suggest that we tighten the compatibility policy a bit:
1. While striving for maximum compatibility is a good thing, we should not feel obliged to stay compatible with expired versions of Python and modules/libraries. 
2. Especially for the heavily used libraries `numpy`, `scipy`, and `matplotlib`, the version requirements should be stated clearly in the documentation (README, Wiki).
3. We might add a version check at initialization, that emits a warning (and recommendation to upgrade) if the minimal requirements are not fulfilled.
4. For optional modules/libraries, a version that does not fulfil the minimal requirements should be treated as if it is not loaded.

title: Inaccurate band characters lead to incorrect CNP
description:
The determination of subband characters might be inaccurate: The number of nodes can be incorrect, or the orbital type E/L/H. If this happens, the determination of the charge neutrality point (CNP, aka 'zero gap') can yield an incorrect result without error message.

The subband character determination appears to fail more frequently for states at high energies and if an electrostatic potential is applied.

*Possible solutions:*
*  The counting of wave function nodes may be made more robust.
*  Try a better heuristic for determining E or L subband character.
*  Try alternative methods for determining the CNP. For example: do not consider states at too high energy; use a simplified algorithm based on position of H1 band and presence of band inversion; relax distinction between E or L.
*  Better detection of failed CNP determination. Possibly a configuration option that sets strictness.

title: Proposal: Multiple values for targetenergy
description:
*Proposal*:\
Allow multiple values for `targetenergy` and do the diagonalization at each given value. Then stitch the eigenvalues and eigenstates together.

*Motivation*:\
Currently, stitching multiple datasets is possible with `kdotpy merge`, but this script does not do much postprocessing.
Presently, @lbovkun would like to calculate transitions for a large energy range. This is not possible with `kdotpy merge` because transitions require the eigenvectors. Doing the calculation with a single `targetenergy` may require an unfeasible number of eigenstates, e.g. `neig 1000` or even more. Doing multiple diagonalizations *might* be computationally less demanding.

*Possible implementation*:\
For each k or B value, iterate the diagonalization function over all values of `targetenergy`. Then stitch /merge the results together. Do a check whether the energy ranges overlap; if not, raise an error or warning. Return the 'merged result' as a single `DiagDataPoint`. All following processing, like calculating transitions, band alignment, etc. will be performed as usual.

*Comments*:
 * Which `targetenergy` values have to be chosen is very hard to predict, so we leave it to the user to choose the values manually.
 * The tolerance required for stitching will depend on the diagonalization method. For example, the GPU accelerated method uses a lower precision than `eigsh` from SciPy. The optimal values will have to be determined by trial and error.
 * In the initial implementation, we use a single value for `neig` applied to all diagonalizations, but in the future we may add the option for different values, i.e., to iterate over pairs of values `(targetenergy, neig)`.

title: kdotpyrc permission error / write_config warning
description: I encountered multiple warnings and an "permission" error when using the command line `python kdotpy-ll.py temp 1.6 8o msubst CdTe mlayer HgCdTe 68% HgTe HgCdTe 68% llayer 85 68 45 zres 0.25 b 0 10 // 50 erange -100 100 nll 20 neig 1000 targetenergy -40 split 0.01 obs llavg legend char noax transitions plotstyle auto cardens -0.005 0.005 / 0.0005 dos out _b50_noax_Q3263 outdir ..\kdotpy-data\Q3263` on a Windows 10 machine and on `master` branch. After postprocessing finished the following error was raised (terminal displayed `21/21` right before) which stopped code execution. Resulting in missing plots for some of the carrier densities, only 15 out of 21 `transitions-filtered_...` plots were generated. I had similar issues when running the command above with `bia` instead of `noax`. All of this is probably related to how parallelization is handled by Windows.

title: Broadening documentation not in line with code if only `temp` is set
description:
If the arguments `broadening` or `dostemp` are not set, but `temp` is set, the code uses a `None` type broadening function, instead of a thermal distribution. This is not in line with the current state of documentation in the wiki (e.g. see entry 'dostemp'), which says that `dostemp` or `broadening` only overwrites `temp` if they are given and otherwise the `temp` argument is used.

Also the `broadening` argument could be made more flexible to take `temp` directly, if `broadening thermal` is given, instead of requiring to specify the temperature a second time. 

~~Furthermore, the current interpretation of `broadening x thermal (auto)` is quite unphysical in LL mode, as it will be automatically scaled with magnetic field. The automatic mode should actually choose `const` in case of `thermal`~~.

title: In-plane magnetic field application is inconsistent
description:
## Issue description
The way in-plane magnetic fields are applied to the Hamiltonian in `kdotpy-2d` and `kdotpy-ll` are currently inconsistent. For both scripts, the in-plane magnetic field is applied during the SymbolicHamiltonian construction in `hb.h1z()` and is taken from the `PhysParams` instance.

Now this instance only holds `magn` values derived from the first entry of a magnetic field vector list. Only this value is used to account for the in-plane magnetic field orbital effect (while for the Zeeman energy, the exchange coupling and the B_z orbital effect it is calculated separately for each B point).

This leads to situations which will not be transparent for users. Consider the following examples:

| cmdargs| in-plane B considered (T)|
| ------ | ------ |
| `b 0 10 / 100 bperp 0.1`| 0.1|
| `b 0 10 / 100 btheta 1`| 0|
| `b -10 10 / 100 bperp 0.1`| 0.1|
| `b -10 10 / 100 btheta 1`| -0.1745|

## Suggested solution
In-plane magnetic fields should be evaluated in a similar way as the Zeeman Hamiltonian via the `b` parameter of the Hamiltonian, not derived from the `params` PhysParams instance. Adding the `b` parameter to the `hb.h1z()` signature and using this instead of `params.magn` should probably be enough to cover the variable B part via the symbolic `MagneticHamiltonian`.

title: get_zero_point() and bandalignment fails with error when using a constant in-plane field and variable B vector
description:
When calculating a magnetic field dependence with an additional constant (in-plane) field contribution (e.g. with `kdotpy-ll.py b 0 12 // 89 bperp 0.1`), bandalignment fails with `Warning (estimate_charge_neutrality_point): Could not determine charge neutrality point: No data at k=0.` as the `DiagData.get_zero_point()` method **fails to find any true zero point**.

As a consequence, `kdotpy` raises a `ValueError: Desired energy e0 should have a numerical value, not None.` during bandalignment and not any output at all is generated.

Even if the determination of band characters and the CNP may fail, the remaining postprocessing should still run through without bandalignment data.

In my test case, the H-bands character could still be determined correctly, but E-bands had been labeled '??', explaining, why the automatic CNP determination failed. For smaller in-plane magnetic fields the determination of band characters and the CNP may still be possible at k=0, but as of the current state of `DiagData.get_zero_point()`, it can not be transferred to the main diagonalization result.

In some scenarios data points are missing in the pdf plot output for polar k-space plots (radial at certain angles). This depends on the number of angular grid points (e.g. 45, 90, but fine with 180) and did not occur in my tests when not requesting an observable colormapping but using the default coloring by energy values. Other `obs` arguments than `orbitalrgb` have not been tested yet.

title: DOS validity range incorrect
description:
The validity range for the (integrated) density of states, shown as red shaded areas where the result is not valid due to missing states, does not yield the expected result.

*Example:*
```
kdotpy 2d 8o noax msubst CdZnTe 4% mlayer HgCdTe 68% HgTe HgCdTe 68% llayer 7 7 7 zres 0.25 split 0.01 k 0 0.5 / 25 erange -60 20 dos
```
The present result shows that a lower bound of validity at E ~ -55 meV. This is the energy of a local minimum of the first valence subband. However, the dispersion of this band is cut off at E ~ -50 meV at the maximum momentum $`k = 0.5\ \mathrm{nm}^{-1}`$. The lower bound of validity should be at this energy, because states in the range -55 meV < E < -50 meV for $`k > 0.5\ \mathrm{nm}^{-1}`$ have not been counted.

*Possible solution:*\
The value and gradient of the dispersion at the edge of the momentum range needs to be taken into account.

title: Berry curvature name and unit in LL mode
description:
The "Berry curvature" that is calculated in LL mode is not really Berry curvature, but the Chern number, where the integral over momentum is implicit.

The observable `berryz` is defined with units of `nm^2`, which is appropriate for momentum mode (e.g., `kdotpy-2d.py`). However this unit is invalid for the LL mode, where `berryz` represents the Chern number which is dimensionless. (The extra factor of `nm^-2` comes from the implicit momentum integration.)

*Possible solution:*\
Define a separate observable for the Chern number. This requires some changes to the postprocessing functions as well.

One might also consider renaming the output files with the 'misleading' name `berry` being replaced by `chern`.

I suggest keeping the command-line argument `berry`, but possibly create an alias `chern`.

title: (Local) integrated observable calculation may not use bandindices
description:
I was looking into the calculation of `berry-int` plots and found the use of `integrated_observable(data, 'berry', local=True)`.

This function uses the band index (`<0|>0`) explicitly to factor in the 'sign' of the observable, depending on 'electron' or 'hole' character.
However, the band index is only a valid indicator for e/h character in special cases[^1]. Especially in LL mode with 'band' crossings interpreted as anticrossings by the bandalign algorithm, it is highly dangerous to rely on the band index for anything else than counting bands to determine the CNP.

I'd like to remind of the discussion in #4, specifically the sign(bindex) & CNP plot in https://git.physik.uni-wuerzburg.de/wbeugeling/kdotpy/-/issues/4#note_7529.

I'm not quite sure yet, whether it's ok to check whether the (LL) band is above or below the neutral energy (CNP), like it is done for determination of charge density and ECP, or if we'd need to go with something like a strict band alignment (probably required for the separate integration of spin up and down states).

[^1]: In the tutorial case on use of `berry` a QW is used: The sign of the bandindex is almost reliably here, as states stay mostly on either side of the band gap, except the crossing of "-2" and "0" LLs in the topological case.\
-In `noax` or `bia` mode these crossing states are band aligned in one run and at the (anti)crossing point the band index flips between both bands, so the energetically higher band will always have a positive sign and the one below the CNP has a negative sign.\
-In `axial` mode, bandalignment is done separately for each LL, so there are individual bandindices. For the two crossing LLs, there is no chance of the band index to change here, for large magnetic fields (after the crossing point) the signs of the band indices are reverted with respect to the bands' positions towards the CNP. But even though the individual e/h band berry curvatures are now calculated wrongly, the summation cancels the error in this case.\
For more complex cases, e.g. thick layers with vanishing gap between valence band and interface states and heavy overlap of their LLs, this is not guaranteed, especially when `bia` comes into play.

title: Modelling of disorder broadening
description:
Currently `kdopty` models disorder boardening using a Gaussian with standard deviation $`\sigma = \sigma_{1\mathrm{T}} \sqrt{B[\mathrm{T}]}`$. This means that the broadening of states increses with magnetic fields. The motivation for such a broadening goes back to refs. [^NovikEA2005] & [^AndoT1982].

However, ref [^AndoT1982] actually distinguishes between short and long range scattering as origin of the disorder broadening (Chapter VI.A.1, p.536ff).

- In the limit of short range scattering, i.e. scattering potential length scales $`d << l`$ (the magnetic length/ cyclotron orbit): $`\sigma^2 = \frac{2 \hbar^2 \omega_c}{\pi \tau} \propto B`$
- In the limit of long range scattering with respect to cyclotron orbit radii: $`\sigma^2 = 4 \langle (V(r) - \langle V(r)\rangle)^2\rangle`$, which is constant w.r.t. $`B`$.

In the HgTe samples I measured in optics, the transition FHWM is constant at about <0.3meV for samples with good mobilities.

The sample investigated in ref. [^NovikEA2005]  (Fig. 4) is a rather old MnHgTe sample with very high intrinsic charge density of $`3.5\times10^{12} \mathrm{cm}^{-2}`$. It is plausible, that in such a case the short range scattering is more suitable, but one should not generally use this broadening scaling also for modern high quality samples.

[^NovikEA2005]: Novik, E. G., Pfeuffer-Jeschke, A., Jungwirth, T.  *et al.* [Phys. Rev. B **72**, 035321 (2005)](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.72.035321)
[^AndoT1982]: Tsuneya Ando, Alan B. Fowler, and Frank Stern [Rev. Mod. Phys. **54**, 437 (1982)](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.54.437)

Attention to: @lwang, @tkiessling, @lbovkun

description:
When using plotstyle normal (that should only plot E vs k points) I get additional vertical lines between some dots (examples in comment below attached).

title: Discontinuous density(z) around LL crossing
description:
Whenever the 'zero Landau levels' cross, there is a discontinuity in the density-as-function-of-z $`\rho(z)`$ with respect to magnetic field B.

Example:
```sh
kdotpy ll zres 0.2 llayer 5 7 5 mlayer HgCdTe 0.68 HgTe HgCdTe 0.68 b 0 9 // 60 erange -60 0 targetenergy -40 neig 50 nll 6 8o msubst CdZnTe 4% obs llindex outdir densztest legend char split 0.01 dos localdos cardens 0 dostemp 4 broadening 1 densityz
```

![bdependence-density](/uploads/1c3cda123a725ba30f1be531c59a34dd/bdependence-density.png)\
Landau fan of a 7 nm quantum well. The black line is the constant-density contour for n = 0.

![densz-44-45](/uploads/04cb6614d5ecf1e0c6aff48030dcaef9/densz-44-45.png)
Comparison of $`\rho(z)`$ for two B field values near the crossing at $`B = B_c`$. Note that the 'function profiles' for electrons and holes are exchanged.

*Diagnosis*:\
The assumption is made that at the charge neutrality point the density is uniformly zero (not taking into account broadening). States that lie above the CNP are considered to be electrons, those below holes. (These have positive and negative band index, respectively.)

At the crossing, the two Landau levels change position. On the left, the H1 band is above n = 0 and 'counted as electrons', while the E1 band is below n = 0 and 'counted as holes'. On the right, the order is opposite, H1 below = holes and E1 above = electrons. The net charge density $`\rho(z) = \rho_h(z) - \rho_e(z)`$ thus flips sign going from $`B < B_c`$ to $`B > B_c`$.

Note that the electron and hole density integrated over z $`n_e = \int \rho_e(z) dz`$ and $`n_h = \int \rho_h(z) dz`$ are exactly equal in magnitude, $`n_h = -n_e`$, so the total density $`n=n_h+n_e`$ vanishes. These quantities are *not* discontinuous near the crossing.

Also other densities are affected by the discontinuity at the crossing for n = 0. That is, a similar discontinuity can be observed at $`B=B_c`$ for $`n\ne 0`$. (Try the example with `cardens -0.001`, for example.)

*Problem*:\
I suspect that this problem is also a cause for the self-consistent calculation to behave poorly. A similar problem was reported in issue #4.

Note that the problem is not a bug in the implementation, but potentially a flaw in the assumptions underlying the modelling.

*Possible solution*:\
This discontinuity seems unphysical, so perhaps the assumption that at n = 0 the density is uniformly zero is not valid. How should $`\rho(z)`$ change if one sweeps the magnetic field across $`B_c`$?

title: Non-linear spacing for layer grid and wavefunctions
description:
I've just been thinking about the influence of the `zres` parameter on performance and accuracy of the Hamiltonian diagonalization.

I remember, that a while ago (when I experimented with `kdotpy-1d` for the first time), I tried increasing solution speed by choosing a lower resolution. While up to a certain critical point this did not notably change the output, above this point observables like the orbital character changed drastically.

As the wavefunctions and their derivatives change really slowly inside the HgTe layer (one often does not calculate bands with more than 5-20 extrema), the sharp kinks at the layer interfaces and decay to zero in the barriers would arguably need a higher resolution, such that the discrete first and second derivatives are still well aproximated at that point.

We should check whether we can introduce something like an adaptive grid spacing for the discrete `z` (and in case of 1D also `y`) dimension, that is narrow for few points around interfaces and can be much rougher inside the well.

E.g. for a 100nm thick layerstack, we could be able to reduce the number of grid points along z from 400 (0.25nm resolution) to something like 120 points (4 x 10 points at interfaces (0.25nm) + 80 points in the remaining layerstack (~1nm)).

title: Landau level weights as observables
description:
### Feature request
For llmode full I'd like to habe additional observables giving the weight of each LL to the eigenstate. This is similar to the orbital contribution observables `gamma<X>`.

### Caveats
Adding this as observable for each LL, this adds `nll` observable columns to the output file, which could lead to 30-200% increased output size with usual values for `nll`. Calculation of these observables should be activated via `config` or cmdarg similar to `overlaps`.

One could limit the number of output LL weights to the dominant n LLs or only LLs with x% minimal weight to reduce the output size. This could result in a single column dict-like output (e.g. in JSON format). Downside: Minimally larger overhead for data parsing. But JSON is widely supported and human readable.

title: Save all eigenvectors to file
description:
### Feature suggestion

Save all eigenvectors in a suitable file format (due to possible large size, a binary format would be recommendable).\
This enables users to do some more/additional postprocessing on "old" calculations, e.g. detailed analysis of wavefunctions or transitions filtered at different densities, without redoing the full calculation.

### Possible implementations

This could be loaded e.g. by `kdotpy-merge` (with a single output.xml) and suitable command line arguments to trigger the new plots. New per DDP postprocessing is currently not supported by this script.

A workaround to make such a workflow possible at the moment is to use the `tempout` and `resume` command arguments (not merged merged from `cuda-solver` branch yet). Some additional flag is still required to keep the eivecs in all DDPs, as well as an option to resume the calculation correctly with a new postprocessing.
However, the temporary output is not intended for long term storage of data!

title: Symmetry lowering effects in kdotpy
description:
`kdotpy` already explicitly accounts for bulk inversion asymmetry (#11), if requested. 

How is the inclusion of further symmetry lowering effects like structure/interface inversion asymmetry (SIA (=Rashba) / IIA) handled? 

As far as I understood from Winklers book, both terms only play a role in the presence of electric potentials. Is this included already in the potential Hamiltonian or do we need to add those terms separately?

Background:\
Especially the SIA term adds further $`k_\pm`$ terms to the Hamiltonian this could give rise to further optical transitions. THz measurements show low photon energy features, almost independent of magnetic field, which get stronger with positive gate voltage and rising electron density in the HgTe layer. I would expect SIA to be a possible candidate for a cause of this feature.
